policy_title: Achieve a zero-carbon economy through energy transition and green investment

verdict.plain: This policy could lower energy bills in the long run by expanding cheap renewables, but the transition involves large upfront costs and real risks of short-term price rises — especially if ending nuclear and fossil fuels creates supply gaps before renewables can fill them. Whether households end up better or worse off depends heavily on how the transition is managed.
verdict.biggest_unknown: Whether the rapid phase-out of nuclear and fossil fuels can be matched by renewable build-out fast enough to avoid a supply gap that forces reliance on expensive gas imports and drives up bills.

verdict.rationale: The long-run case for cost-of-living improvement is grounded in the CCC's assessment that full decarbonisation costs less than continued fossil fuel dependence — particularly given exposure to fuel price shocks that have historically hammered household bills. A successful build-out of cheap onshore and offshore wind, plus solar, could materially reduce wholesale electricity prices and insulate households from global gas markets. The policy's stated investment of £40bn/year, though far above OBR's modelled government share, could accelerate this. However, the near-term risks to household costs are substantial and well-evidenced. The renewable targets are far more ambitious than current trajectories: offshore wind needs to scale from 18GW to 80GW, solar from 17GW to 100GW, onshore wind from well below 35GW to 53GW. Supply chain and grid connection bottlenecks are already severe — the grid connection queue is four times the 2030 capacity needed, and twice as much transmission infrastructure must be built in five years as in the past decade. Any shortfall in build-out, combined with the ending of North Sea production and the phase-out of nuclear (which experts warn could force more gas use), risks a supply gap that would push bills up, not down, in the medium term. The mandatory financial divestment by 2030 adds further uncertainty for pension-holders. The balance of evidence points to genuine long-run gains if delivery succeeds, but serious transition risks to affordability if it does not — hence a mixed verdict. The dominant uncertainty is delivery speed versus the pace of fossil fuel and nuclear exit.

sources.quote: Green MPs will push the next government to stop all new fossil fuel extraction projects in the United Kingdom and to cancel recently issued fossil fuel licences, such as for Rosebank. We will also end all subsidies to the oil and gas industries. The UK’s current climate targets do not reflect the urgency of the climate crisis or what is required by global justice. We would push the government to transition to a zero-carbon society as soon as possible, and more than a decade ahead of 2050. Green MPs will aim to introduce new support and incentives to directly accelerate wind energy development...This will pave the way for wind to provide around 70% of the UK’s electricity by 2030. Our targets are to achieve 80GW of offshore wind, 53 GW of onshore wind, and 100 GW of solar by 2035. We will end the de-facto ban on onshore wind. We are committed to the energy sector being under local democratic control as far as is possible. We will push for: • A minimum threshold of community ownership in all sustainable energy infrastructure. • The removal of regulatory barriers to community energy. • Investment in community energy by regional investment banks. The Crown Estate will be brought into public ownership and should open more coastal waters for offshore wind and marine energy. Control over its assets within the jurisdiction of Wales should be devolved to the Welsh Government, as it is in Scotland. There needs to be a just transition, led by workers and unions, that sees communities reap the rewards of the shift to green energy. As part of this, we will push the next government to establish an Offshore Energy and Skills Passport so that workers can transition more easily between offshore energy industries. Elected Greens will push for: • Investment in skills and training (including retrofitting) reaching £4bn per year, allowing workers to be prepared for the transition and the new roles they can take on. Elected Greens will seek to significantly expand and improve the efficiency of the electricity grid, increasing its capacity so that it can distribute the increased electricity the UK will need as it transitions away from fossil fuels. We would connect our electricity supply more closely to that of our neighbours in Europe to provide a broader-based supply we can call on when needed and to allow us to export electricity when we have a surplus. We would rapidly expand the capacity for energy storage, so that there is security of electricity supply for short-term peaks in demand and periods of low supply from variable renewables. We would cease development of new nuclear power stations, as nuclear energy is much more expensive and slower to develop than renewables. Green MPs will campaign to phase out existing nuclear power stations. Elected Greens would push for significant investment in a green economic transformation, alongside the private sector. This programme to include: • An average of £40bn per year over the course of the next parliament, including £7bn annually on climate adaptation. Any company holding a UK banking licence will be required to present an investment strategy outlining a clear pathway to divestment of its current fossil fuel assets as soon as possible, and at least by 2030. The Bank of England’s mandate will be changed so that funding the sustainability transition becomes a central objective, alongside the maintenance of price stability. Non-bank financial institutions, such as UK pension funds, investment funds, mutual funds, brokers and insurance companies that sell policies in the UK, will need to remove fossil fuel assets from their investment portfolios, securities transactions and balance sheets by 2030. Green MPs will back the setting up of regional mutual banks to drive investment in decarbonisation and local economic sustainability by supporting investment in SMEs and community-owned enterprises and cooperatives. These banks will be capitalised through a Cooperative Development Fund using some of the funds made available through the United Kingdom Infrastructure Bank (UKIB), along with an additional £10bn of public money. We will give local authorities £2bn per year to provide grants to help businesses decarbonise. We will explore legal ways for companies to be transformed into mutual organisations, especially at the point of succession from one owner to another. Green MPs will seek to increase investment into research and development by over £30bn in the lifetime of the five-year parliament. Additional spending will be primarily focused on tackling the climate and environmental crisis through funding research into sectors including: energy storage; agroecological agriculture and soil health; re-use, repair, recycling and designing out waste; carbon neutral construction; carbon-neutral production and carbon capture technology.

blocking_issues.detail: E3 (CCC claim) is described as a 'measurable' baseline in the evidence snippet but the verdict correctly tiers it as 'projected'. However, E3 is backed partly by energy-uk.org.uk (industry body) and the claim paraphrases CCC advice without a direct CCC source URL — the entailment is reasonable but the sourcing is thin for a projected claim supporting the positive cost-of-living case.

E5 (Greenpeace: removing subsidies projected to reduce global CO2 by 5% by 2030) is from an advocacy source and is not used in the verdict's claims — correctly omitted. No blocking issue, but worth noting the verdict avoids this weak source.

E25 is backed by bdonline.co.uk and iea.org; bdonline is an architecture trade publication, not a primary IEA source. The claim as stated ('Phasing out existing nuclear...would create a significant energy gap') is well-supported by the IEA co-citation and the quote entails the claim, but the primary source quality is moderate.

verifier.notes: The verdict is well-structured and the mixed direction is genuinely supported by claims on both sides: long-run cost reduction case (E3, renewable build-out) versus near-term supply gap and transition risk (E4, E19, E20, E25). The magnitude and time horizon are consistent with the evidence. No tier_integrity violations detected — projected claims are correctly labelled. The biggest_unknown is specific and non-lazy. No party identity leakage. No lever_leakage — the verdict consistently frames everything through household energy cost and affordability. Minor sourcing quality warnings noted but none blocking.

evidence.snippet: Transition to a zero-carbon society more than a decade ahead of 2050, by ending all new fossil fuel extraction projects and cancelling recent licences like Rosebank, and ending all subsidies to the oil and gas industries. This includes accelerating wind energy development to provide around 70% of UK electricity by 2030, with targets of 80GW offshore, 53GW onshore, and 100GW solar by 2035, and ending the de-facto ban on onshore wind. The plan involves expanding community and public ownership of energy infrastructure, removing regulatory barriers, investing in community energy via regional banks, and bringing the Crown Estate into public ownership. A just transition will be supported with £4bn per year investment in skills and training for workers in carbon-intensive industries to transition to green jobs, and the establishment of an Offshore Energy and Skills Passport. The electricity grid will be significantly expanded and improved, with increased capacity for energy storage and closer connection with Europe. The policy also calls for ceasing development of new nuclear power stations due to high costs and phasing out existing ones. Overall, an average of £40bn per year will be invested over the next parliament in a green economic transformation, including £7bn annually on climate adaptation, involving public and private sector participation. Financial services will be required to divest from fossil fuel assets by 2030, and the Bank of England's mandate will include funding sustainability. Regional mutual banks will be set up with £10bn public money to invest in SMEs and community-owned enterprises for decarbonisation, supplemented by £2bn per year in grants for businesses from local authorities. Investment in R&D will increase by over £30bn across five years, focusing on climate and environmental solutions like energy storage, agroecological agriculture, and carbon-neutral construction.

evidence.snippet: The UK is legally committed to achieving net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050
Emissions in 2020 were 51% below 1990 levels, partly due to the COVID-19 pandemic

The Climate Change Committee (CCC) has consistently advised on the pathways and costs to meet the 2050 target, noting that decarbonising the UK by 2050 would ultimately cost less than continued reliance on fossil fuels, especially considering potential future price shocks

However, some analysts argue that forcing a premature decline in North Sea production could increase reliance on imported fossil fuels, which may have higher associated emissions, and lead to a loss of tax revenues and jobs in the supply chain

Removing these subsidies is projected to directly reduce global CO2 emissions by an estimated 5% by 2030 and would make renewable energy sources significantly more attractive to investors and consumers
The current government's ambition for onshore wind is 27-29GW by 2030, with a potential to exceed 35GW by 2035 in an optimistic scenario
The policy's target of 53GW onshore wind by 2035 is considerably more ambitious than current government projections
*   **Offshore Wind:** The UK currently has around 18GW of offshore wind capacity
The government's current ambition is to deploy up to 50GW of offshore wind by 2030, including up to 5GW from floating offshore wind
There is a total potential pipeline of 93GW for offshore wind in the UK
Achieving 80GW offshore by 2035 would represent a substantial acceleration, requiring the offshore wind workforce to increase from 40,000 to between 75,000 and 94,000 by 2030-2035
This growth is considered essential for meeting clean power targets, but challenges remain in the supply chain and skills pipeline
*   **Solar Energy:** As of June 2024, the UK had 16.9GW of solar capacity online

The current government's Clean Power 2030 Action Plan aims for 45-47GW of solar PV capacity by 2030, with a potential to reach around 85GW by 2035 with additional policies, particularly for rooftop solar

Meeting this target would likely require significant expansion of large-scale ground-mounted solar farms, which currently occupy less than 0.1% of the UK's land, increasing to approximately 0.6% to meet net-zero targets

*   **Crown Estate Public Ownership:** The Crown Estate manages the seabed around England, Wales, and Northern Ireland, leasing it for offshore wind development and generating significant profits (over £1 billion in 2024/25)
Greenpeace has criticised the Crown Estate for "monopoly profiteering" and driving up costs for offshore wind developers and energy bill payers
Currently, the Crown Estate is a statutory corporation, with its Scottish equivalent already devolved and managed by Crown Estate Scotland

*   **Grid Expansion and Storage:** Grid access is a major challenge for offshore wind development, with the current queue of projects waiting to connect reaching four times the capacity needed for 2030 targets
The National Energy System Operator (NESO) calculates that meeting 2030 targets will require twice as much transmission network to be built between 2025-2030 as in the previous decade
Significant investment in grid infrastructure and energy storage is essential to integrate high levels of intermittent renewable energy and ensure system reliability
Most existing reactors are nearing the end of their operational lives and are expected to cease generation by around 2028-2030, with Sizewell B potentially operating until 2055

*   **Expert Disagreement:** Many experts and institutions, including the International Energy Agency (IEA), argue that nuclear energy is indispensable for achieving net-zero emissions cost-effectively and for providing reliable, low-carbon baseload power, especially as electricity demand is forecast to almost double over the next 25 years
They highlight that a significant halt in nuclear construction in past decades has cost Britain dearly in carbon emissions and energy security

Phasing out existing nuclear and ceasing new development would create a significant energy gap, making net-zero ambitions harder and potentially more expensive, possibly forcing increased reliance on gas to maintain grid stability
The existing nuclear fleet has contributed over £123 billion to the UK economy and supported 31,000 jobs annually
While building new nuclear is expensive, some argue it is cheaper to run per kilowatt-hour than most other power sources except wind

The Boston Consulting Group estimated that Britain would need to spend between £700 billion and £900 billion over five years (i.e., £140-180 billion per year) to revamp its energy infrastructure alone to reach net-zero by 2050

The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) estimated the net cost to the whole economy of reaching net-zero between 2025 and 2050 at £116 billion, with the government bearing around 36% of these costs, or approximately £9.9 billion per year

The proposed £40 billion per year is a substantial investment, significantly higher than the government's estimated share of direct costs identified by the OBR, and would represent a major boost to green industries, job creation, and economic growth

*   **Climate Adaptation (£7bn/year):** The CCC estimates that investment in adaptation across the UK needs to be around £11 billion per year, with a range of £7-22 billion per year, equivalent to approximately £380 billion over 2025-2059
Currently, the extent of public investment in adaptation is unclear due to a lack of unified reporting
*   **Financial Services Divestment by 2030:** The Bank of England has noted that divesting from fossil fuels does not have a statistically significant impact on overall portfolio performance

However, some analysts warn that mandatory, blanket divestment could create costs for beneficiaries (e.g., pension schemes) by reducing the investment opportunity set and could lead to less scrupulous investors acquiring these assets, without necessarily driving real-economy decarbonisation
Engagement with companies is often cited as a more effective mechanism for driving corporate action
Local government pension funds in the UK still held about £10 billion in fossil fuel investments in 2021

The proposed policy goes further by requiring sustainability to be a *central objective* alongside price stability, and to include credit guidance (directing lending towards a sustainability transition, with bans or ceilings for unsustainable activities)
